screens.title: Collision Detection and Triggers
screens.narratorSegment: Interactions between objects are the lifeblood of a game. In this lesson you will learn the two foundational components — Colliders and Rigidbodies — and how Unity uses them to detect both physical collisions and non-physical trigger events. We’ll see the callback methods Unity provides, such as the collision callbacks that deliver impact details, and the trigger callbacks that simply indicate overlap. You will get concrete examples: destroying an enemy on impact, collecting a coin with a trigger, and a small 2D lab to test wall collisions and coin collection. You’ll also learn practical filters: Tags for quick identification in code and Layer Masks for efficient selective collision. Understanding these pieces prevents common issues like missed events or using the wrong 2D/3D callback variants. By the end, you’ll be able to choose between a solid collider that blocks motion and a trigger that senses presence without halting movement, and you’ll know the rule of thumb about when a Rigidbody is required. Consider how a healing zone should behave: should it stop the player or let them pass while applying effects? That question will help you pick collisions or triggers.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Collision Detection and Triggers
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Collision Detection and Triggers

Learn how Unity tells when objects hit or overlap, and how to respond with reliable C# callbacks that drive gameplay events.

Collider
Defines shape used for interactions.
Rigidbody
Makes an object respond to physics.
Triggers
Detect overlap without blocking motion.
In this lesson

You will inspect OnCollision and OnTrigger callbacks, practice a 2D coin collection lab, and learn Tag and Layer Mask patterns to keep detection efficient.

Explore Key Topics
Colliders & Types
Box, Sphere, Capsule, Mesh — choose for shape and performance.
Callbacks
OnCollisionEnter/TriggerEnter and their stay/exit pairs.
Filtering
Tags for identity; Layers for performance and selective ignoring.
Visual Concept
R
Rigidbody + Collider
Physical interaction, collisions can block motion.
T
Collider as Trigger
No block; overlap events only.
Why it matters

Correctly choosing colliders, rigidbodies, and trigger settings determines whether your game objects respond naturally to physics or simply signal events — both are essential tools for responsive gameplay.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of the first objectives screen you will be able to name and differentiate Unity’s two collision building blocks: Colliders and Rigidbodies. You will understand why a Collider alone does not produce physics interactions and when adding a Rigidbody makes an object respond to gravity and impacts. You will also be introduced to the three primary collision callbacks: the initial contact event, the continuous contact event, and the exit event, and why the Collision parameter gives you contact points and references to the other object. Finally on this screen you will see how triggers differ: they register overlap without physically blocking motion and use a Collider parameter rather than collision details. Each objective includes a short example so you can picture when you would use that callback in a real game, and a small mnemonic to help you remember that triggers are for presence while collisions are for impact. These objectives form the conceptual foundation you will apply in the hands-on 2D lab.

screens.title: Colliders: shapes that define interaction
screens.narratorSegment: A Collider is the shape Unity uses to detect interactions. It does not by itself cause physics motion; it simply outlines the volume where interactions are considered. Common types include BoxCollider, SphereCollider, CapsuleCollider, and MeshCollider. Box and sphere colliders are the most performant and work well for many gameplay objects. MeshColliders are useful for complex geometry but can be costly and should be used sparingly or in convex/simplified forms. In practice, pick the simplest collider that reasonably fits your object: for a crate use a box, for a ball use a sphere, and for a character use capsule colliders to approximate posture. Remember that without any collider, a GameObject will pass through others and no collision or trigger callbacks will fire. A frequent misconception is assuming colliders automatically apply physics — they do not. If you want physics-based motion, attach a Rigidbody. As an example, a coin prefab used for collection typically has a collider marked as Is Trigger, no Rigidbody, and that allows a player with a Rigidbody to pass through while still generating trigger events. Think about shape, performance, and whether the collider should block motion or only sense presence when you choose a type.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Colliders
Definition & Roles

A Collider defines the geometric volume used for collision and trigger detection. Alone it does not move objects; it only participates in detection. Choose a collider type based on shape and performance needs.

BoxCollider
Good for crates, walls, tiles. Fast and simple.
SphereCollider
Best for balls and round pickups.
MeshCollider
Use sparingly for complex static geometry.
Concrete Example
A coin prefab should have a small circle or box collider marked Is Trigger and usually no Rigidbody. The player, which has a Rigidbody, will still generate OnTriggerEnter events when passing through the coin. This avoids physical blocking while allowing collection logic to run.
Key Takeaway

Colliders define detection volumes. Combine them with Rigidbodies when you want physics responses; mark as trigger when you only want overlap events.

Common Mistake: Assuming colliders add gravity or motion. They do not; add a Rigidbody for physics.

screens.title: Rigidbodies: enabling physics behavior
screens.narratorSegment: A Rigidbody makes a GameObject respond to forces, gravity, and collisions. The important rule to remember is that for a physical collision to be registered between two colliders, at least one of the objects involved must have a Rigidbody. If both objects are static colliders with no Rigidbody, they will pass through one another with no callbacks. If one has a Rigidbody and the other does not, the Rigidbody object will be affected by the collision and will not pass through the static collider. If both have Rigidbodies, they will physically interact and can bounce or apply impulses to each other. Use Rigidbodies on objects that need movement controlled by the physics engine, like moving platforms, projectiles, or the player. For kinematic controlled objects, set Rigidbody to kinematic when you want scripted motion that still registers collisions in certain setups. A common misconception is to add Rigidbodies to everything; unnecessary Rigidbodies add overhead and can complicate deterministic behavior. A better approach is to add a Rigidbody only to objects that need physics responses and keep static environment geometry without Rigidbodies for stability and performance.

keyIdea.text: At least one Rigidbody is required for collision callbacks; add rigidbodies only to objects that need physics-driven motion.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Rigidbodies
How they affect collisions
Rigidbodies enable physics responses and determine whether collisions are treated as physical impacts. Three common cases: both objects static (no Rigidbody) -> no collisions fired; one Rigidbody -> Rigidbody hits static collider; both Rigidbodies -> full physics interaction.
Static vs Dynamic
Static colliders for environment, dynamic rigidbodies for moving objects.
Kinematic Rigidbody
Use for scripted motion where you control transforms but still want some collision callbacks.
Concrete Example
A player with a Rigidbody2D colliding into a static wall's BoxCollider2D will cause OnCollisionEnter2D on the player. If the wall had a Rigidbody2D, the physics engine would resolve forces between them, which is useful for movable obstacles but not necessary for fixed walls.
Key Takeaway

Add Rigidbodies to objects you want physics to move. Keep static geometry without Rigidbodies to avoid unnecessary physics overhead.

screens.title: Collision callbacks: enter, stay, exit
screens.narratorSegment: Unity provides three main collision callbacks for physical collisions: OnCollisionEnter, OnCollisionStay, and OnCollisionExit. OnCollisionEnter is called a single time when two colliders first come into contact; it’s the right place to trigger a one-off response like applying damage, playing a hit sound, or destroying an object on impact. OnCollisionStay is called every physics update while colliders remain in contact; use it for sustained effects like continuous damage from standing on a hazard or applying friction-like behavior. OnCollisionExit fires once when the colliders separate, useful for stopping effects you started during stay, such as turning off a hazard or ending a sound. Each callback receives a Collision parameter that supplies contact points, relative velocity, and a reference to the other GameObject so you can inspect tags, layers, or components. A typical pitfall is doing expensive work inside OnCollisionStay without rate-limiting; remember it runs frequently. Also ensure you use the correct 2D variants for 2D physics: OnCollisionEnter2D, OnCollisionStay2D, OnCollisionExit2D. Practice writing a handler that logs the first contact and performs a simple action, and then extend it for a sustained effect during OnCollisionStay.

keyIdea.text: OnCollisionEnter: first contact; OnCollisionStay: continuous contact; OnCollisionExit: separation. Use Collision parameter for details.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Collision Callbacks
Process Steps
1
OnCollisionEnter: Called once at first contact. Use for one-time responses like damage or sounds.
2
OnCollisionStay: Called repeatedly while contact persists. Use for continuous effects but avoid heavy work every frame.
3
OnCollisionExit: Called once on separation. Use to stop effects started during stay.
Example Handler
using UnityEngine;

public class CollisionHandler : MonoBehaviour
{
  void OnCollisionEnter(Collision collision)
  {
    if (collision.gameObject.CompareTag("Enemy"))
    {
      Debug.Log(gameObject.name + " collided with an Enemy!");
      Destroy(collision.gameObject);
    }
  }
}
Key Takeaway

Use the appropriate enter/stay/exit callbacks for one-off actions, continuous effects, and cleanup respectively; watch for performance in Stay.

screens.title: Trigger callbacks: sensing overlap without blocking
screens.narratorSegment: Triggers let you detect when something enters or remains in an area without physically stopping it. To make a Collider act as a trigger, check Is Trigger in the Inspector. When a collider is a trigger, objects will pass through it but Unity will call OnTriggerEnter, OnTriggerStay, and OnTriggerExit. These methods take a Collider parameter rather than Collision because there is no contact point data. Triggers are ideal for collecting items, starting cutscenes, or creating zones like healing areas where the player should not be bounced back. The golden rule for triggers is similar to collisions: at least one of the interacting GameObjects must have a Rigidbody for trigger events to be delivered. A typical example from the lab is a Coin prefab with an Is Trigger collider and no Rigidbody, and a Player with a Rigidbody2D; when the player overlaps the coin, OnTriggerEnter2D fires and you can destroy the coin. A common mistake is forgetting to check Is Trigger or forgetting the Rigidbody requirement — both result in no events. Always use the 2D variants for 2D colliders. Trigger callbacks: sensing overlap without blocking means mark colliders as triggers to detect presence without blocking; ensure at least one rigidbody is present for events to fire.. In practical terms, using ontriggerenter, ontriggerstay, and ontriggerexit for non-physical interactions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Triggers
Trigger Behavior

Triggers do not produce physical contact. They signal presence. Use them to pick up items, create zones, or activate logic without stopping motion.

Is Trigger: checkbox makes a collider report overlap events instead of blocking motion.
Parameter: OnTrigger callbacks use a Collider parameter because collision contact data is not available.
Example: Coin Pickup
using UnityEngine;

public class CoinCollector : MonoBehaviour
{
  void OnTriggerEnter2D(Collider2D other)
  {
    if (other.CompareTag("Coin"))
    {
      Debug.Log("Coin Collected: " + other.gameObject.name);
      Destroy(other.gameObject);
    }
  }
}
Key Takeaway

Triggers detect presence without blocking movement. Use them for pickups, zones, and any non-physical event detection.

screens.title: Collision vs Trigger: choosing the right tool
screens.narratorSegment: Deciding between a collision and a trigger depends on whether you want to physically block the object or only detect its presence. Use collision callbacks when objects must physically interact: characters bumping into walls, projectiles hitting enemies, or physics-based reactions where momentum and contact points matter. Use trigger callbacks when you want to sense that something entered a zone without hindering motion, such as picking up coins, entering a healing area, or toggling a cinematic trigger. A helpful contrast: collisions give you a Collision parameter with contact points and impact force, which lets you apply damage proportional to impact or compute bounce directions. Triggers give a simpler Collider parameter, which is sufficient for identification and activation. A typical mistake is marking a collider as trigger when you expected a physical response, or forgetting to use the 2D/3D variants. Another practical tip: if your zone must allow free passage and also detect presence, pick trigger; if you want to prevent passage, use a non-trigger collider with Rigidbody combinations configured appropriately. Collision vs Trigger: choosing the right tool means choose collisions for physical blocking and triggers for sensing presence; use callback parameters accordingly.. In practical terms, when to block motion and when to sense overlap. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Collision vs Trigger
Collision (Physical)
  • Blocks movement
  • Provides Collision parameter with contact details
  • Use for impacts, damage on hit, and bounce behavior
Trigger (Overlap)
  • Does not block movement
  • Provides Collider parameter for identification
  • Use for pickups, zones, and activation areas
Concrete Scenario

Implement coins as triggers so the player walks through them and collects them. Implement walls as non-trigger colliders so the player cannot pass through.

screens.title: Implementing OnCollisionEnter and OnTriggerEnter

The collision handler uses OnCollisionEnter or its 2D variant to detect a physical impact. The Collision parameter gives you access to the other GameObject and contact information. Use CompareTag for efficient identification, then apply game logic like playing a sound, applying damage, or destroying the other object. public class CollisionHandler : MonoBehaviour
{
  void OnCollisionEnter(Collision collision)

Trigger (2D)
using UnityEngine;

public class CoinCollector : MonoBehaviour
{
  void OnTriggerEnter2D(Collider2D other)

    if (other.CompareTag("Coin"))

      Debug.Log("Coin Collected: " + other.gameObject.name);

    }

Pro tip

When destroying objects in callbacks, perform all logic needed first. Accessing properties after Destroy may raise exceptions. Also use CompareTag instead of name comparisons for speed and safety.

screens.title: Common mistakes and how to fix missed events
screens.narratorSegment: Missed collisions and triggers are some of the most common issues newcomers face. Use a short checklist when events don’t fire. First, check Rigidbody presence: at least one object in the interaction must have a Rigidbody for collision or trigger callbacks. Second, verify Is Trigger is checked when you expect trigger events — forgetting this turns a trigger into a physical collider. Third, confirm you used the correct 2D or 3D callback variants; using OnTriggerEnter when working with 2D colliders will not fire events. Fourth, ensure you are using CompareTag rather than fragile name comparisons, and that the tag exists and is assigned correctly. Fifth, inspect whether objects are on layers that ignore each other via Layer Collision Matrix in Project Settings — your layers may be configured to prevent collisions. Finally, avoid destroying an object and then trying to access it later in the same method. If an event still fails, add simple Debug. Log statements at the top of your callback to test whether the method runs at all. These checks will resolve most issues quickly. Common mistakes and how to fix missed events means verify rigidbody presence, is trigger, correct 2d/3d methods, tags, layers, and order of destroy calls.. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Troubleshooting
Quick Checklist
  • Does at least one object have a Rigidbody?
  • Is the collider set to Is Trigger when expecting trigger events?
  • Are you using the 2D method variants for 2D colliders?
  • Is the tag correctly assigned and compared with CompareTag?
  • Are layers configured to ignore the interaction in Project Settings?
Example Fix

If OnTriggerEnter2D is not firing for coins, check that the coin collider has Is Trigger checked and the player has a Rigidbody2D. Add a Debug.Log at the start of the method to confirm whether the method is invoked at all.

Common Mistake

Destroying the other object before applying score or state can lead to missing references. Always record necessary data before Destroy.

screens.title: Tags and Layer Masks for efficient filtering
screens.narratorSegment: Tags and Layer Masks are complementary tools for filtering collision and trigger logic. Tags are string labels you assign to GameObjects and are ideal for simple identity checks in code, like checking if an object is a "Coin" or "Enemy" using CompareTag. Layer Masks group objects into integer-indexed layers so Unity’s physics engine can ignore or allow collisions between layers via the Layer Collision Matrix. Use tags to answer the question "what is this object?" and layers to answer "which groups should interact?" Layers are also used in raycasting to restrict which objects are considered. A practical pattern is to tag individual prefabs for quick script checks and put broad categories like "Player", "Enemy", or "Hitbox" on layers to configure collision behavior globally. Misuse comes when people overuse tags for performance-sensitive filtering; for frequent collision filtering it’s more efficient to use the physics layer matrix. In short, use CompareTag for per-event identity checks and configure Layer Masks to avoid unnecessary collision checks across the entire physics system. Tags and Layer Masks for efficient filtering means use tags for identification in code and layers for global selective collision control and performance optimization.. In practical terms, using tags for identity and layers for collision performance. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Tags & Layer Masks
Tags

Assign human-readable labels like "Coin" or "Enemy". Use CompareTag("TagName") in scripts for fast identity checks.

Tip: CompareTag is more efficient and safer than comparing object name strings.
Layer Masks

Layers let you group objects to configure which layers interact using the physics collision matrix. They are also used to filter raycasts with LayerMask parameters.

Pattern: Use layers for global collision rules and tags for per-object identity checks in callbacks.
Key Takeaway

Tags identify; layers group. Use both together to keep detection accurate and efficient.

screens.narratorSegment: Let's apply what you've learned with a short assessment scenario. Imagine GameObject A has a BoxCollider and a Rigidbody, and GameObject B has a BoxCollider but no Rigidbody, with Is Trigger unchecked. If A moves into B, what happens and which callback runs? This illustrates the rule that at least one object must have a Rigidbody for a physical collision, and that a non-trigger collider will block motion. fullNarratorScript:
Interactions between objects are the lifeblood of a game. In this lesson you will learn the two foundational components — Colliders and Rigidbodies — and how Unity uses them to detect both physical collisions and non-physical trigger events. We’ll see the callback methods Unity provides, such as the collision callbacks that deliver impact details, and the trigger callbacks that simply indicate overlap. You will get concrete examples: destroying an enemy on impact, collecting a coin with a trigger, and a small 2D lab to test wall collisions and coin collection. You’ll also learn practical filters: Tags for quick identification in code and Layer Masks for efficient selective collision. Understanding these pieces prevents common issues like missed events or using the wrong 2D/3D callback variants. By the end, you’ll be able to choose between a solid collider that blocks motion and a trigger that senses presence without halting movement, and you’ll know the rule of thumb about when a Rigidbody is required. Consider how a healing zone should behave: should it stop the player or let them pass while applying effects? That question will help you pick collisions or triggers.

By the end of the first objectives screen you will be able to name and differentiate Unity’s two collision building blocks: Colliders and Rigidbodies. You will understand why a Collider alone does not produce physics interactions and when adding a Rigidbody makes an object respond to gravity and impacts. You will also be introduced to the three primary collision callbacks: the initial contact event, the continuous contact event, and the exit event, and why the Collision parameter gives you contact points and references to the other object. Finally on this screen you will see how triggers differ: they register overlap without physically blocking motion and use a Collider parameter rather than collision details. Each objective includes a short example so you can picture when you would use that callback in a real game, and a small mnemonic to help you remember that triggers are for presence while collisions are for impact. These objectives form the conceptual foundation you will apply in the hands-on 2D lab.

On this objectives screen we focus on what you will practice. You will implement OnCollisionEnter2D and OnTriggerEnter2D in a small 2D scene: a player with a Rigidbody2D and BoxCollider2D, walls with colliders that block motion, and coins that are triggers. You will write scripts that log collisions and destroy collected coins, and you will test the scene to observe which callbacks fire. You will also practice checking tags efficiently with CompareTag rather than comparing names, and you will assign layers to objects so you can later configure selective collision behavior. Finally you will run simple troubleshooting checks: verify that at least one object has a Rigidbody, confirm the Is Trigger checkbox when expecting trigger events, and make sure you use the 2D variant of the callbacks for 2D physics. These practical skills ensure your game objects behave predictably and save time debugging missed events.

A Collider is the shape Unity uses to detect interactions. It does not by itself cause physics motion; it simply outlines the volume where interactions are considered. Common types include BoxCollider, SphereCollider, CapsuleCollider, and MeshCollider. Box and sphere colliders are the most performant and work well for many gameplay objects. MeshColliders are useful for complex geometry but can be costly and should be used sparingly or in convex/simplified forms. In practice, pick the simplest collider that reasonably fits your object: for a crate use a box, for a ball use a sphere, and for a character use capsule colliders to approximate posture. Remember that without any collider, a GameObject will pass through others and no collision or trigger callbacks will fire. A frequent misconception is assuming colliders automatically apply physics — they do not. If you want physics-based motion, attach a Rigidbody. As an example, a coin prefab used for collection typically has a collider marked as Is Trigger, no Rigidbody, and that allows a player with a Rigidbody to pass through while still generating trigger events. Think about shape, performance, and whether the collider should block motion or only sense presence when you choose a type.

A Rigidbody makes a GameObject respond to forces, gravity, and collisions. The important rule to remember is that for a physical collision to be registered between two colliders, at least one of the objects involved must have a Rigidbody. If both objects are static colliders with no Rigidbody, they will pass through one another with no callbacks. If one has a Rigidbody and the other does not, the Rigidbody object will be affected by the collision and will not pass through the static collider. If both have Rigidbodies, they will physically interact and can bounce or apply impulses to each other. Use Rigidbodies on objects that need movement controlled by the physics engine, like moving platforms, projectiles, or the player. For kinematic controlled objects, set Rigidbody to kinematic when you want scripted motion that still registers collisions in certain setups. A common misconception is to add Rigidbodies to everything; unnecessary Rigidbodies add overhead and can complicate deterministic behavior. A better approach is to add a Rigidbody only to objects that need physics responses and keep static environment geometry without Rigidbodies for stability and performance.

Unity provides three main collision callbacks for physical collisions: OnCollisionEnter, OnCollisionStay, and OnCollisionExit. OnCollisionEnter is called a single time when two colliders first come into contact; it’s the right place to trigger a one-off response like applying damage, playing a hit sound, or destroying an object on impact. OnCollisionStay is called every physics update while colliders remain in contact; use it for sustained effects like continuous damage from standing on a hazard or applying friction-like behavior. OnCollisionExit fires once when the colliders separate, useful for stopping effects you started during stay, such as turning off a hazard or ending a sound. Each callback receives a Collision parameter that supplies contact points, relative velocity, and a reference to the other GameObject so you can inspect tags, layers, or components. A typical pitfall is doing expensive work inside OnCollisionStay without rate-limiting; remember it runs frequently. Also ensure you use the correct 2D variants for 2D physics: OnCollisionEnter2D, OnCollisionStay2D, OnCollisionExit2D. Practice writing a handler that logs the first contact and performs a simple action, and then extend it for a sustained effect during OnCollisionStay.

Triggers let you detect when something enters or remains in an area without physically stopping it. To make a Collider act as a trigger, check Is Trigger in the Inspector. When a collider is a trigger, objects will pass through it but Unity will call OnTriggerEnter, OnTriggerStay, and OnTriggerExit. These methods take a Collider parameter rather than Collision because there is no contact point data. Triggers are ideal for collecting items, starting cutscenes, or creating zones like healing areas where the player should not be bounced back. The golden rule for triggers is similar to collisions: at least one of the interacting GameObjects must have a Rigidbody for trigger events to be delivered. A typical example from the lab is a Coin prefab with an Is Trigger collider and no Rigidbody, and a Player with a Rigidbody2D; when the player overlaps the coin, OnTriggerEnter2D fires and you can destroy the coin. A common mistake is forgetting to check Is Trigger or forgetting the Rigidbody requirement — both result in no events. Always use the 2D variants for 2D colliders. Trigger callbacks: sensing overlap without blocking means mark colliders as triggers to detect presence without blocking; ensure at least one rigidbody is present for events to fire.. In practical terms, using ontriggerenter, ontriggerstay, and ontriggerexit for non-physical interactions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Deciding between a collision and a trigger depends on whether you want to physically block the object or only detect its presence. Use collision callbacks when objects must physically interact: characters bumping into walls, projectiles hitting enemies, or physics-based reactions where momentum and contact points matter. Use trigger callbacks when you want to sense that something entered a zone without hindering motion, such as picking up coins, entering a healing area, or toggling a cinematic trigger. A helpful contrast: collisions give you a Collision parameter with contact points and impact force, which lets you apply damage proportional to impact or compute bounce directions. Triggers give a simpler Collider parameter, which is sufficient for identification and activation. A typical mistake is marking a collider as trigger when you expected a physical response, or forgetting to use the 2D/3D variants. Another practical tip: if your zone must allow free passage and also detect presence, pick trigger; if you want to prevent passage, use a non-trigger collider with Rigidbody combinations configured appropriately. Collision vs Trigger: choosing the right tool means choose collisions for physical blocking and triggers for sensing presence; use callback parameters accordingly.. In practical terms, when to block motion and when to sense overlap. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Let's walk through two concise C# templates you'll use frequently: a collision handler and a trigger handler. The collision handler uses OnCollisionEnter or its 2D variant to detect a physical impact. The Collision parameter gives you access to the other GameObject and contact information. Use CompareTag for efficient identification, then apply game logic like playing a sound, applying damage, or destroying the other object. For pickups and zones, use OnTriggerEnter or the 2D variant with a Collider parameter; check the tag and then apply effects such as increasing score and destroying the pickup. A common pitfall is destroying the object before performing all necessary logic — perform actions like scoring or state changes before Destroy to avoid missing references. Also be mindful to use the correct method signatures for 2D versus 3D. Practice copying these templates into your project and testing each by observing console logs and behavior in the scene. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Second, verify Is Trigger is checked when you expect trigger events — forgetting this turns a trigger into a physical collider. Fifth, inspect whether objects are on layers that ignore each other via Layer Collision Matrix in Project Settings — your layers may be configured to prevent collisions. Tags and Layer Masks are complementary tools for filtering collision and trigger logic. Tags are string labels you assign to GameObjects and are ideal for simple identity checks in code, like checking if an object is a "Coin" or "Enemy" using CompareTag. Layer Masks group objects into integer-indexed layers so Unity’s physics engine can ignore or allow collisions between layers via the Layer Collision Matrix. Use tags to answer the question "what is this object?" and layers to answer "which groups should interact?" Layers are also used in raycasting to restrict which objects are considered. A practical pattern is to tag individual prefabs for quick script checks and put broad categories like "Player", "Enemy", or "Hitbox" on layers to configure collision behavior globally. Misuse comes when people overuse tags for performance-sensitive filtering; for frequent collision filtering it’s more efficient to use the physics layer matrix. In short, use CompareTag for per-event identity checks and configure Layer Masks to avoid unnecessary collision checks across the entire physics system. Here are the core concepts to keep in mind. First, a Collider defines the shape used for physics interactions; without it objects cannot collide or trigger events. Second, a Rigidbody makes objects subject to physics and is required on at least one object for collision callbacks to occur. Third, a Collision is a physical interaction that can block movement and provides a Collision parameter with contact details. Memorize these three because they are the foundation of both collisions and triggers. Use these succinct definitions as a checklist when debugging: does the object have a collider? does at least one object have a Rigidbody? is the collider marked as trigger or not?
